title: Plant Transport System
seo_title: Primary 5 Science: Plant Transport System Worksheets (with Answers)
standard_text: Identify the plant transport system: water-carrying tubes carry water and mineral salts from the roots to the other parts of the plant, and food-carrying tubes carry food from the leaves to the other parts. Investigate the movement of water in a plant and the effects of removing the food-carrying tubes (summary of the MOE Primary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Primary 5 science worksheets for Singapore pupils on the plant transport system: water-carrying and food-carrying tubes, coloured-water experiments and ring-barking. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Water goes up; food goes to every part.
body_html:
How to think about it

A plant has two kinds of transport tubes.

  • Water-carrying tubes carry water and mineral salts from the roots, up the stem, to all parts of the plant.
  • Food-carrying tubes carry food made in the leaves to all parts of the plant (up and down).
  • Water is lost from the leaves, so more water is drawn up from the roots.
  • Ring-barking removes the food-carrying tubes in the outer layer: food collects above the ring and the roots slowly starve.
Example

A ring of bark is removed from a tree. Which part swells?

The food-carrying tubes are cut

Food moving down collects above the ring

Answer: The part above the ring.

Example

A white flower is put in blue water. Why do the petals turn blue?

Coloured water enters the stem

It travels up the water-carrying tubes

Answer: Water is carried up to the flower.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking food is carried only upwards. It goes to all parts, including the roots.
  • Mixing up the two kinds of tubes.
  • Thinking ring-barking stops water reaching the leaves at once. The water-carrying tubes are deeper inside.
  • Thinking roots can make their own food.

faq.q: What do the water-carrying tubes carry?
faq.a: Water and mineral salts, taken in by the roots, up the stem to all the other parts of the plant.

faq.q: What happens when a tree is ring-barked?
faq.a: The food-carrying tubes in the outer layer are removed. Food collects and the stem swells above the ring, the roots get no food and the tree slowly dies.

faq.q: Why do leaves stay green for a while after ring-barking?
faq.a: The water-carrying tubes are deeper inside the stem and are not removed, so water still reaches the leaves.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Where does it go after the roots?
items.e: Water: soil → roots → stem → leaves.

items.q: Which tubes carry water to the leaves for making food?
items.e: The water-carrying tubes carry water and mineral salts from the roots to the other parts.

items.q: Why are the transport tubes compared to the blood vessels of animals?
c: Both carry substances to all parts of the living thing.
items.e: The plant transport system moves water and food.

items.q: In which direction do the water-carrying tubes carry water?
c: upwards, from the roots to the leaves
items.e: Water moves up from the roots.

items.q: Which tubes carry water up the stem?
items.e: The water-carrying tubes carry water and mineral salts from the roots to the other parts.

items.q: Which tubes carry food made in the leaves?
items.e: The food-carrying tubes carry food from the leaves to the other parts.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Where does it go after the soil?
items.e: Water: soil → roots → stem → leaves.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Where does it go after the stem?
items.e: Water: soil → roots → stem → leaves.

items.q: What do the water-carrying tubes carry?
c: water and mineral salts from the roots to the other parts
items.e: They run from the roots, up the stem, to the leaves.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Which does the water pass through first: the air or the soil?
c: Water does not pass through either.
They happen at the same time.
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Where does it go after the leaves and flowers?
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: What do the food-carrying tubes carry?
c: food from the leaves to the other parts of the plant
items.e: Food is carried up and down.

items.q: In which direction is food carried?
c: to all parts of the plant, up and down
items.e: Food goes to roots, fruits, seeds and growing tips.

items.q: Which tubes carry coloured water to the petals of a white flower?
items.e: The water-carrying tubes carry water and mineral salts from the roots to the other parts.

items.q: Which tubes carry mineral salts from the roots?
items.e: The water-carrying tubes carry water and mineral salts from the roots to the other parts.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Which does the water pass through first: the leaves and flowers or the soil?
c: They happen at the same time.
Water does not pass through either.
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: Which tubes carry food to the developing seeds?
items.e: The food-carrying tubes carry food from the leaves to the other parts.

items.q: Which tubes carry sugar to a ripening mango?
items.e: The food-carrying tubes carry food from the leaves to the other parts.

items.q: Why do the roots need food from the leaves?
c: Roots need food to make light.
Roots cannot make food because they have no chloroplasts and get no light.
items.e: All living cells need food.

items.q: Food moves from the leaves to the roots. Where does it go after the leaves?
items.e: Food: leaves → stem → roots (and to fruits, seeds and growing parts).

sets.title: Water and food in the plant

items.q: Why does a farmer water plants at the roots, not on the leaves?
c: Water on leaves turns to food.
The roots take in water and the water-carrying tubes carry it up.
Leaves take in water through their tubes.
items.e: Water enters the plant through the roots.

items.q: A mango fruit ripens and becomes sweet. Where did the sugar come from?
c: the leaves, through the food-carrying tubes
items.e: Food made in the leaves is carried to the fruit.

items.q: A pot plant's leaves droop on a hot day. What will help it most?
items.e: Roots take up the water.

items.q: A plant in a pot with no drainage holes is watered too much. Why might its roots rot?
c: Roots like lots of standing water.
Soggy soil has no air for the roots.
items.e: Roots need air too.

items.q: A tree is very tall. How does water reach the top leaves?
c: It does not reach the top.
Rain falls straight into the top leaves only.
It travels up tiny tubes in the trunk.
items.e: A trunk is a stem.

items.q: Why does a plant wilt on a hot day?
c: It loses water from its leaves faster than it takes in water.
items.e: Wilting means the cells have too little water.

items.q: Food moves from the leaves to the roots. Where does it go after the stem?
items.e: Food: leaves → stem → roots (and to fruits, seeds and growing parts).

items.q: Ethan put a Chinese cabbage leaf in blue-coloured water for a day. Why would the colour move up faster on a hot, windy day?
c: More water is lost from the leaves, so more water is drawn up.
items.e: Water loss from the leaves pulls water up the stem.

items.q: Arjun put a Chinese cabbage leaf in blue-coloured water for a day. Where would the colour be seen first?
c: in the stem, just above the water
at the tips of the leaves
items.e: Water moves up from the bottom of the stem.

items.q: Where are the mineral salts in the soil taken in?
items.e: They are carried up with the water.

items.q: Cut flowers in a vase stay fresh longer if you trim their stems. Why?
c: It stops the flowers growing roots.
A fresh cut lets water travel up the stem more easily.
items.e: Fresh tubes take up water.

items.q: Where does most of the water leave a plant?
c: through tiny holes in the leaves, into the air
items.e: Water evaporates from leaves.

items.q: Daniel put a celery stalk in green-coloured water for a day. The stem was then cut across. What do the coloured spots show?
items.e: The coloured water travels up the water-carrying tubes.

items.q: Which tubes carry food down to the roots?
items.e: The food-carrying tubes carry food from the leaves to the other parts.

items.q: Why do the leaves of a cut flower droop after a few hours out of water?
c: The petals take all the food.
No water is reaching the leaves through the water-carrying tubes.
The flower makes too much food.
items.e: The stem has no water supply.

items.q: Aisha put a white chrysanthemum in green-coloured water for a day. Where would the colour be seen first?
c: at the tips of the leaves
in the stem, just above the water
items.e: Water moves up from the bottom of the stem.

items.q: Jia Hui put a white chrysanthemum in red-coloured water for a day. Why would the colour move up faster on a hot, windy day?
c: More water is lost from the leaves, so more water is drawn up.
items.e: Water loss from the leaves pulls water up the stem.

items.q: Xin Yi put a white chrysanthemum in red-coloured water for a day. What does the experiment show?
c: Water is carried up the stem to the leaves and flowers.
Food is carried down to the roots.
Leaves take in water from the air.
items.e: The colour travels with the water.

items.q: Why do leaves feel cooler than the air on a hot day?
c: Water evaporating from them cools them down.
items.e: Like sweat.

items.q: Which part of a plant stores food carried by the food-carrying tubes?
items.e: Food is carried down and stored.

items.q: A ring of the outer layer of bark was removed from the trunk of a young tree (ring-barking). After some weeks, the trunk just above the ring swelled. Why?
c: Food carried down from the leaves collected above the ring.
The tree grew new roots there.
items.e: The food-carrying tubes were cut, so food could not pass the ring.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Which does the water pass through first: the stem or the roots?
c: Water does not pass through either.
They happen at the same time.
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: Hui Min put a celery stalk in red-coloured water for a day. What does the experiment show?
c: Leaves take in water from the air.
Water is carried up the stem to the leaves and flowers.
Food is carried down to the roots.
items.e: The colour travels with the water.

items.q: A ring of the outer layer of bark was removed from the trunk of a young tree (ring-barking). Which part of the tree swells?
c: the part just below the ring
the part just above the ring
items.e: Food moving down cannot pass the ring.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Where was the water just before it reached the leaves and flowers?
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: A ring of the outer layer of bark was removed from the trunk of a young tree (ring-barking). Which tubes were removed?
items.e: The food-carrying tubes are near the outside of the stem; the water-carrying tubes are deeper inside.

items.q: A ring of the outer layer of bark was removed from the trunk of a young tree (ring-barking). Can the leaves still make food?
c: No, the leaves die at once.
No, the leaves need the bark to make food.
Yes, for a time, because they still get water and light.
items.e: The problem is that the food cannot reach the roots.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Where was the water just before it reached the stem?
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Which does the water pass through first: the leaves and flowers or the stem?
c: Water does not pass through either.
They happen at the same time.
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: Arjun stood a white daisy in a jar of water with blue food colouring. What does this investigation show?
c: Water travels up the stem to the leaves and flowers.
Water travels down from the leaves to the roots.
Leaves take in water from the air.
items.e: The colour is a way of seeing where the water goes.

items.q: A ring of the outer layer of bark was removed from the trunk of a young tree (ring-barking). Why does the tree eventually die?
c: The bark grows back too fast.
The tree gets too much food.
The roots die without food, so water and mineral salts can no longer be taken in.
The leaves get no water at once.
items.e: First the roots starve; then the whole tree suffers.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Which does the water pass through first: the air or the roots?
c: They happen at the same time.
Water does not pass through either.
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: Aisha stood a white rose in a jar of water with green food colouring. Why does the colour spread up the plant?
c: The plant takes up the coloured water through tiny tubes in its stem.
The colour floats up through the air.
items.e: The tubes carry water up from the bottom.

items.q: A ring of the outer layer of bark was removed from the trunk of a young tree (ring-barking). Why do the leaves stay green for some time?
c: The leaves take in water from the air.
The water-carrying tubes deeper inside are not cut, so water still reaches the leaves.
items.e: Only the outer layer was removed.

items.q: Hafiz stood a white carnation in a jar of water with blue food colouring. Where will the blue colour appear after a day?
c: nowhere, the colour stays in the jar
only at the bottom of the stem
items.e: The coloured water travels up the stem to the top of the plant.

items.q: Mei Ling put a Chinese cabbage leaf in red-coloured water for a day. The stem was then cut across. What do the coloured spots show?
items.e: The coloured water travels up the water-carrying tubes.

items.q: Imran stood a white rose in a jar of water with purple food colouring. When the stem is cut across, what will Imran see?
c: a purple stem all the way through, like paint
small purple dots, which are the ends of the water tubes
items.e: The tubes carry the water up the stem.

items.q: Rachel stood a white tulip in a jar of water with blue food colouring. Why does the colour spread up the plant?
c: The colour floats up through the air.
The plant takes up the coloured water through tiny tubes in its stem.
items.e: The tubes carry water up from the bottom.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Where does it go after the stem?
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: Farah stood a white lily in a jar of water with red food colouring. Where will the red colour appear after a day?
c: only at the bottom of the stem
nowhere, the colour stays in the jar
items.e: The coloured water travels up the stem to the top of the plant.

items.q: Which way does water travel in a plant?
c: up, from the roots to the leaves
down, from the leaves to the roots
items.e: Roots are at the bottom.

items.q: A plant is pulled up and its roots are washed clean of soil. Why might it wilt after replanting?
c: Many tiny root hairs were damaged, so it takes in less water.
Roots do not take in water.
Soil is not needed for water.
items.e: Root hairs take in water.

items.q: What are root hairs for?
c: taking in water from the soil
items.e: Tiny hairs on the roots.

items.q: Why is food colouring used in the celery investigation?
c: so we can see where the water goes
items.e: Water is clear.
